papers.title: A brief training session in language switching offers immediate benefits for inhibitory control among English-dominant bilinguals
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study investigated whether a short-term training session in language switching enhances inhibitory control in English-dominant bilinguals ( N = 55) whose second language backgrounds included 17 various languages. The participants completed a pre-training flanker task, a 50-minute numeral-based language-switching task and a post-training flanker task. Results showed significantly reduced flanker effect following the language-switching task. In the switching task, participants exhibited typical switch cost patterns, with slower and less accurate responses on switch trials compared to nonswitch trials. Additionally, switch costs were asymmetrical, with greater costs observed into their first versus second language, consistent with inhibitory control accounts of bilingual language use. Overall, these findings suggest that language switching engages control processes that can have immediate, positive effects on inhibitory control outside the language domain. These results support partial overlap between bilingual language control and domain-general executive processes, highlighting the context-dependent nature of cognitive transfer effects.
papers.authors: Karolina Rachwal, Celina Del Vecchio, John W. Schwieter

papers.title: Bilingualism shapes neural control: Distinct experiences predict conflict monitoring and sustained attentional control
papers.abstract_text: Abstract The present study used event-related potentials to examine how bilingual experiences shape neural responses to contextual cues and conflict resolution. Fifty bilingual undergraduates completed a context-specific proportion congruency (CSPC) Stroop task while electroencephalography was recorded. Greater L2 usage was associated with reduced conflict effects, consistent with more efficient control. The N2 was larger for incongruent than congruent trials and varied by context, with lower L2 proficiency associated with greater context-dependent increases in N2 amplitude, whereas higher proficiency was associated with more stable responses. The conflict slow potential showed that earlier L2 acquisition was associated with greater sustained attentional resource availability across contexts. Together, these findings indicate that processing efficiency is reflected in how control demands are distributed across early and late stages of processing. More broadly, bilingual experiences shape distinct neural control profiles, highlighting the importance of interpreting behavioral and neural measures jointly.
papers.authors: John G. Grundy, Aslı Yurtsever, Kaiah Sotebeer

papers.title: Classifier congruency effects in Spanish–Chinese noun phrase production: Behavioral and electrophysiological evidence
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Mandarin Chinese employs a classifier system requiring classifiers obligatorily positioned between demonstratives or numerals and nouns in noun phrases (NPs; e.g., 一张桌子 , [one specific-classifier-zhang1 table] , ‘one table’). While classifier congruency effects have been documented in monolingual Chinese speakers, it remains unclear whether such effects extend to early Spanish–Chinese bilinguals. This study examined classifier congruency effects in NP production by 29 early Spanish–Chinese bilinguals and 30 Mandarin Chinese speakers using behavioral and electroencephalography (EEG) measures. Participants completed picture-word interference (PWI) tasks with four conditions, manipulating classifier congruency (congruent versus incongruent) and semantic relatedness (related versus unrelated). Behaviorally, both groups showed significantly longer naming latencies for classifier-incongruent and semantically related conditions. Event-related potential (ERP) results revealed N400-like effects for classifier incongruency in both groups. For semantic interference, N400-like effects were observed in bilinguals and P600-like effects were observed in Chinese speakers. This study provides the first behavioral and ERP evidence that classifier features are automatically activated in bilingual NP production, suggesting the robustness of classifier congruency effects in early Spanish–Chinese bilinguals.
papers.authors: Ruixue Wu, Maria del Carmen Parafita Couto, Niels O. Schiller

papers.title: Cross-linguistic impacts on morphological awareness and vocabulary: Comparing Chinese-English bilingual and English monolingual preschoolers
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Bilingualism changes language and literacy development, with morphological awareness and vocabulary as fundamental skills. This study tested whether experience with Chinese, which primarily uses compounds and lacks affixes, creates distinct pathways for acquiring English compound and affix awareness, thereby shaping their associations with English vocabulary. We tested Chinese-English-bilingual and English-monolingual preschoolers ( N = 202, 3-to-5-year-olds) and built two path models. Model 1 included bilinguals and revealed that English affix awareness was primarily explained by cumulative English exposure (% English-input) and associated with vocabulary, while English compound awareness was predicted by Chinese compound proficiency and unrelated to vocabulary. Model 2 compared between groups, revealing significant associations between English vocabulary and both types of morphological awareness for monolinguals, whereas bilinguals only showed significance for affix awareness. Findings suggest that Chinese-English-bilingual and English-monolingual children show distinct morphological development patterns. Importantly, awareness of affixes, a rare feature in Chinese, is crucial for Chinese-English-bilinguals’ English vocabulary.
papers.authors: Xin Sun, Hélène Deacon, Janet F. Werker

papers.title: Cued vs. voluntary language switching in frequent code switchers: behavioral costs and benefits
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Language control in bilinguals is often studied using switch and mixing costs, primarily with bilinguals who separate the languages they speak by context. However, some bilinguals, such as Lebanese Arabic–French speakers, use languages in an integrated manner, by code-switching daily, a pattern captured by language entropy. This study examines language-switching costs and benefits in 62 frequent code switchers (FCS) using cued and voluntary picture-naming tasks. Results showed reduced switch and mixing costs in the voluntary condition compared to the cued condition. Half the participants even exhibited a mixing benefit when switching freely, modulated by L2 proficiency, with more balanced bilinguals showing larger benefits. In line with De Bruin et al. (2018), these findings suggest that less constrained language switching may reduce language control demands, and for FCS, mixing languages can even be easier than having to stay in one. Findings remain to be supported by more ecological discourse-based research.
papers.authors: Layana Awada, Barbara Köpke

papers.title: Developing the productive emotion vocabulary test (PEVT) for adult speakers of English as an additional language
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Emotion vocabulary (EV) is integral to language proficiency, yet it is rarely assessed, and existing tools are largely decontextualised and unvalidated for adult users of English as an additional language (Lx). We introduce the Productive Emotion Vocabulary Test (PEVT), a vignette-based free-recall task eliciting up to three responses. Twenty-two pictorial-text vignettes, redesigned from materials validated with German children, were administered to 107 adults, alongside LexTALE and a language background questionnaire. Eighteen vignettes elicited the target emotion or a close synonym as the dominant response, with substantial naming agreement. In mixed-effects analyses, context length did not affect accuracy, whereas response order, LexTALE and produced-word frequency did: first responses were more likely to be accurate than subsequent responses, and higher LexTALE scores and higher-frequency labels were associated with greater accuracy. Findings provide preliminary validity evidence for the PEVT as a research instrument capturing productive EV breadth and a narrowly operationalised facet of depth: contextual naming alignment.
papers.authors: Csaba Zoltan Szabo, Wei Le Jeremy Bong, Soon Tat Lee, Allen Jie Ein Chee, Yifan Wang

papers.title: Discrete emotion norms for 1,122 English words: A database of categorical ratings by Chinese-English bilinguals
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Although the discrete emotion perspective has gained increasing attention in affective and psycholinguistic research, large-scale normative datasets in a second language (L2) remain limited. To address this gap, the present study introduces a comprehensive database of discrete emotion norms for L2 English. The dataset comprises 1,122 words evaluated by 525 Chinese-English bilinguals across five discrete emotion categories: happiness, anger, fear, disgust and sadness. Participants rated subsets of these words using a 5-point Likert scale. The results demonstrate high inter-rater reliability and reveal systematic relationships between discrete emotion ratings and affective dimensions. Furthermore, these categorical ratings correlate with emotion prototypicality and key psycholinguistic variables, including age of acquisition, word frequency, concreteness and semantic diversity. Distributional analyses highlight a pronounced asymmetry: happiness dominates the semantic space. This database provides detailed discrete emotion ratings for each word and offers a fine-grained tool for selecting controlled stimuli for research on L2 emotion.
papers.authors: Yunhan Si, Chuanbin Ni

papers.title: Does native culture restore emotional intensity? Distinct effects of cultural context on L2 affective processing
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Bilinguals often experience reduced emotional resonance in their second language (L2), known as “emotional distance.” This study investigates how cultural context, specifically culture relatedness, modulates this experience in late Mandarin-English bilinguals. We employed a multi-methodological approach to disentangle implicit and explicit processing. Study 1 (Implicit Association Test) revealed no automatic bias linking culture to emotion, suggesting that long-term L2 immersion may equilibrate implicit associations. Study 2 (explicit ratings), however, found a significant interaction: priming native (Chinese) culture led participants to evaluate negative L2 words as more negative, whereas the L2 (British) cultural context attenuated these evaluations, reinforcing emotional distance. Positive words remained unaffected. These findings demonstrate that culture is an active modulator of bilingual emotion. While acculturation may balance implicit links, conscious activation of native cultural schemas can bridge L2 emotional distance for aversive content, whereas L2 contexts serve to buffer emotional intensity.
papers.authors: Yanxi Lu, Kate Cain, Bo Yao, Francesca Citron

papers.title: Emotional word processing in bilinguals: An oscillatory cascade from perception to regulation in the second language
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Processing emotionally negative words in a second language (L2) feels less vivid and more cognitively demanding than in the first language (L1), yet the neural mechanisms underlying this difference remain poorly understood. Using single-trial modelling of event-related potentials (ERPs) and event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs), we examined attention allocation to negative versus neutral words in highly proficient late Polish–English bilinguals performing a semantic categorisation task in a modified oddball paradigm. Valence and language modulated early posterior negativity (EPN) and P300, but not the N400. Mass-univariate analysis detected valence modulations in the N400 range, highlighting limitations of classic ERP approaches. Time–frequency analysis further revealed Language × Valence interactions: negative L2 words selectively elicited a cascade of delta, theta and alpha synchronisation from posterior to frontal regions across 59–641 ms, consistent with successive perceptual, lexical-semantic and regulatory processing stages. Emotional processing in L2 is thus qualitatively distinct, more effortful and regulated rather than simply being less efficient.
papers.authors: Iga Krzysik, Marcin Naranowicz, Olivia Molina-Nieto, Guillaume Thierry, Rafał Jończyk

papers.title: Extending the in-group advantage: Vocal emotion recognition in first and second languages by Dutch-English bilinguals
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Previous research finds that vocal emotions are recognized above chance, with higher accuracy typically observed for one’s own cultural group – an “in-group” advantage. However, this may not apply uniformly, especially for bilinguals who are highly proficient in a second language (L2) but not members of the L2 cultural in-group. This study investigates Dutch-English bilinguals’ recognition of anger, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral emotion in Dutch (first language; L1), English (second language; L2) and two unfamiliar languages, Arabic and Hindi, using pseudo-utterances. Listeners were highly accurate in recognizing emotions in both Dutch and English. Recognition in Arabic matched their known languages, while Hindi was lower. Additionally, accuracy in English emotion recognition was positively correlated with English proficiency. These results suggest that the in-group advantage can extend to a highly proficient L2, indicating that cultural membership is not strictly necessary for highly accurate vocal emotion recognition.
papers.authors: Adriana R. Miller, Cristal Giorio, Gabrielle Stokes, Susanne Brouwer, Janet G. van Hell

papers.title: Feeling close or distant: The role of the narrator in the Foreign-Language Effect on moral decision-making
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study investigated whether social distance conveyed through the communicative context modulated the Foreign-Language Effect in moral decision-making. Dutch–English bilinguals responded to personal moral dilemmas in Dutch or English, presented in written form (Experiment 1) or spoken form (Experiment 2). In Experiment 3, personal and impersonal dilemmas were presented. Across experiments, a narrator, designed to appear socially close or distant, was introduced midway through the experiments. Contrary to the predictions, no reliable Foreign-Language Effect was observed in any experiment, nor did narrator-based social distance or dilemma type affect moral decisions. These null effects suggest that subtle manipulations of social distance, particularly when conveyed by artificial or unfamiliar narrators, are insufficient to alter moral decisions. These findings establish important boundary conditions for social distance accounts of the Foreign-Language Effect and indicate that stronger emotional engagement or clearer in-group cues may be necessary for language-related shifts in moral decision-making to emerge.
papers.authors: Anna Gorter, Susanne Brouwer

papers.title: Knowing and feeling: The role of semantic valence in emotional prosody perception for L2 Chinese learners
papers.abstract_text: Abstract In Mandarin Chinese, the same acoustic feature, pitch, conveys both semantic valence and emotional prosody. The effects of semantic valence on bilingual emotional prosody perception are mixed, with some studies reporting semantic facilitation and others showing interference. To clarify this, we extend the conceptual account of semantic valence to second language acquisition by examining its two components: learners’ semantic knowledge and the inherent semantic valence of stimuli. We investigated the independent and interactive effects of these components of semantic valence on emotional prosody perception for L1-English L2-Chinese learners in Chinese words and sentences. We found that semantic valence facilitated L2 learners’ perception when congruent with emotional prosody, but interfered when incongruent. Notably, these semantics-prosody (in)congruence effects were significantly predicted by learners’ semantic knowledge. Our results suggest an interaction between linguistic knowledge and paralinguistic perception in bilingual emotion processing.
papers.authors: Cheng Xiao, Jiang Liu, Svetlana V. Shinkareva, Xuan Yang, Rutvik H. Desai

papers.title: L1–L2 similarity and L2 word frequency effects in Chinese
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Competing accounts have been proposed to explain why word frequency effects are often larger in second-language (L2) than in first-language (L1) reading. The lexical entrenchment hypothesis attributes this pattern to weaker lexical representations in L2 due to reduced exposure, whereas the language competition hypothesis predicts that cross-language interference from L1 modulates L2 lexical processing. To test these accounts, we conducted an eye-tracking study comparing native Chinese readers and L2 Chinese readers from alphabetic and Japanese L1 backgrounds. L2 readers exhibited larger word frequency effects than native readers. Critically, the magnitude of L2 word frequency effect did not differ between L1 backgrounds. These findings suggest that L2 word frequency effects are more consistent with differences in lexical entrenchment than with cross-language competition.
papers.authors: Xin Lai, Xin Jiang

papers.title: L2 exposure intensity modulates the time course of verbal humor comprehension: An ERP study
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Understanding verbal humor in a second language (L2) is a hallmark of advanced communicative competence, yet its time course remains unclear. This study investigates the role of L2 exposure intensity in humor comprehension. Forty-two English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners (Intense vs. Limited Exposure) read jokes in which identical punchlines followed humorous or coherent setups and judged funniness. Behavioral results showed that responses were slower to humorous than to coherent endings, and accuracy was higher in the Intense Exposure group than in the Limited Exposure group. ERPs showed a larger N400 to humorous endings compared to coherent endings. A P600 effect to humorous endings was observed in the Intense Exposure group but not in the Limited Exposure group, suggesting greater engagement of reinterpretation under Intense Exposure. These findings support a conditioned two-stage model of L2 humor in which early detection is broadly preserved, whereas later reinterpretation depends on L2 exposure intensity.
papers.authors: Fan Peng, Rong Zhou, Musi Xie

papers.title: Moral identity and language jointly influence how bilinguals feel and decide
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This preregistered study investigated how moral identity relates to moral decisions and emotional responses in 106 Greek–English bilinguals. Participants evaluated two sacrificial-harm and two honesty-based interpersonal moral dilemmas and completed the Moral Identity Questionnaire (Black & Reynolds, 2016, Personality and Individual Differences , 97, 120–129). Analyses combined NHST and Bayesian approaches. Higher moral self and moral integrity scores predicted stronger emotional reactions and more deontological choices, particularly in honesty-based dilemmas. Language did not exert a reliable overall effect on moral decisions. However, participants responding in their first language (L1) reported higher moral self scores than those responding in their second language (L2), whereas moral integrity did not differ across language conditions. Emotional intensity varied by language and dilemma type: participants generally reported stronger emotions in their L2 but experienced stronger emotional intensity in response to sacrificial dilemmas in their L1. A multilevel mediation analysis indicated that emotional intensity did not reliably mediate the relationship between language and moral choices.
papers.authors: Irini Mavrou, Stavroula Mavrou, Andreas Kyriakou

papers.title: Multilingual experience and cognitive control shape lexical competition in non-native word production: An fMRI study
papers.abstract_text: Abstract During production, multilinguals face increased lexical competition within and across languages, demanding cognitive control. This study investigated how multilingual experience—indexed by proficiency and usage—modulates the influence of trait-level (via control tasks) and state-level (using a Stroop-embedded picture naming task) cognitive control on non-native language production. Greater lexical competition was associated with poorer naming performance. Stroop trials showed facilitation for individuals with stronger control abilities but interference for those with weaker abilities, particularly among lower-proficiency participants. Higher English proficiency and more balanced language use were linked to better naming performance. Although proficient multilinguals exhibited larger lexical competition effects, those with more balanced language use demonstrated better adaptation to conflict resolution. Neuroimaging revealed increased activation in language-specific and domain-general regions under high competition, with higher-proficiency individuals dynamically recruiting additional neural resources. Together, these findings show that multilingual experience and cognitive control shape behavioral and neural mechanisms during non-native language production.
papers.authors: Sifan Zhang, Haoyun Zhang

papers.title: Multilingual exposure and lexical–executive abilities underlying verbal fluency: A study of children with and without autism
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Multilingualism provides many benefits for the cognitive and communicative development of non-autistic children, including the development of lexical-semantic abilities. In contrast, the influence of multilingualism is less clear for autistic children, who often experience challenges in the development of language abilities. We present data from 345 autistic and non-autistic children (3–12 years) from semantic and phonemic verbal fluency (VF) tasks. Children’s monolingualism or multilingualism was operationalised as the continuous measure of language exposure entropy. Our study is the first to monitor both semantic and phonemic VF in multilingual autistic children. Non-autistic children show clear benefits of multilingualism for VF emerging with increasing age. For autistic children, there are neither negative nor positive effects of multilingualism on VF. Follow-up analyses reveal that this is independent of the strength of social-communicative autism symptoms. Taken together, our findings reveal that multilingualism is not detrimental for the development of lexical abilities of autistic children.
papers.authors: Anna Czypionka, Pauline Wolfer, Franziska Baumeister, Stephanie Durrleman

papers.title: Native-like orthographic awareness despite limited phonological-semantic development: Evidence from early Chinese-learning bilingual kindergarteners
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Despite growing numbers of bilingual children acquiring Chinese in early childhood, little is known about emergent Chinese literacy before formal instruction. We examined 116 Beijing kindergarteners: 79 early Chinese-learning bilinguals from diverse non-Mandarin L1 backgrounds (ages 2–5) and 37 native Chinese peers (ages 4–5). Experiment 1 revealed asymmetric age-related patterns in the bilingual children: phonological knowledge (character–syllable mappings) was above chance by age 2, while visual-graphic discrimination remained at chance until age 4, then reached near ceiling by age 5. Experiment 2 compared 40 of these children (ages 4–5) with native peers on literacy measures. Bilinguals achieved native-like orthographic awareness ( d = .11) despite significant gaps in word reading ( d = 1.05), vocabulary ( d = 1.13), phonological awareness ( d = 1.29), morphological awareness ( d = 1.33) and rapid naming ( d = 1.28). Vocabulary uniquely predicted reading for both groups ( β = .53), highlighting its critical role in early L2 Chinese literacy.
papers.authors: Anna Gurevich, Li Yin

papers.title: Proficient bilinguals make less superstitious choices revisiting the FLE in light of L2 proficiency
papers.abstract_text: Abstract The relationship between language and other domains of cognition is a key area of interest in bilingualism research. A relevant phenomenon in this regard is the Foreign Language Effect (FLE), which suggests that individuals may make more rational decisions when using a second language (L2) compared to their native language (L1). Here, by replicating a previous study, we investigated how different levels of L2 proficiency influence superstitious beliefs among bilingual individuals, beyond the language (L1 or L2) in which they are tested. Our findings showed no significant differences in superstition levels between the L1 and L2 contexts. However, we found that greater L2 proficiency was linked to lower superstition levels in both languages. These results suggest that L2 proficiency, or variables associated with it, plays a key role in shaping rational decision-making and may lead to inaccurate estimates of the FLE if it is not adequately controlled for. This study advances our understanding of the FLE by emphasising the importance of considering L2 proficiency in research on bilingual cognition and judgement.
papers.authors: Silvia Purpuri, Nicola Vasta, Barbara Treccani, Roberto Filippi, Claudio Mulatti

papers.title: Skilled reading in a second language: Core reading processes, L2 proficiency and first-language background
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study examined incremental processes in skilled second-language (L2) reading by identifying those shared with first-language (L1) reading and those modulated by L1 background and L2 proficiency. Skilled college-level L2 English readers (L1 Spanish, Korean or Chinese) were compared with native English speakers in self-paced reading of New York Times texts. Each word was annotated for word-, sentence- and passage-level predictors to test how these variables shape reading. Both L1 and L2 reading were affected by the same factors, indicating shared incremental processes. In L2, the magnitude of these effects was shaped by proficiency and readers’ L1 background, with the most pronounced differences observed among Chinese–English readers. These findings support a skilled reading acquisition principle: Fluent reading relies on largely shared processes grounded in target-language knowledge and procedural skills for using this knowledge efficiently, even as proficiency and L1 background introduce variation in skilled L2 reading.
papers.authors: Lin Chen, Xiaoping Fang, Charles Perfetti

papers.title: Social bilingual language use is associated with neural efficiency in inhibitory control: Evidence from ERPs
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Cognitive control supports flexible goal maintenance and conflict resolution. Although bilingual experience has been proposed to enhance its efficiency through sustained language control, emerging evidence suggests these effects reflect adaptive recalibration driven by individual language use rather than domain-general transfer. Here we examined how individual differences in bilingual experience modulate behavioral and neural indices of adaptive attentional control during conflict processing, as indexed by an adaptive Flanker task. Fifty participants (M = 19.6 years) completed the Language and Social Background Questionnaire and an electroencephalography adaptive Flanker task. Event-related potentials in the N100, N200 and P300 windows indexed attentional allocation, conflict detection, and monitoring. Behaviorally, participants showed the expected Flanker interference effect, with no modulation by bilingual experience. In contrast, greater Non-English Social Use, but not overall bilingualism or home use, was associated with attenuated N100s and N200s, suggesting reduced early attentional demands. These neural effects, in the absence of behavioral differences, suggest experience-dependent efficiency in control recruitment rather than enhanced control.
papers.authors: Megan Nakamura, Sergio Miguel Pereira-Soares, Allison Roggen, Michele T. Diaz, Eleonora Rossi

papers.title: The effect of contextual richness on L2 learners’ processing and incidental acquisition of non-literal English phrasal verbs: An eye-tracking study
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Many studies have used post-tests to examine word-related factors, such as encounter frequency, that influence L2 learners’ incidental acquisition of single words. However, less is known about how context affects the processing and acquisition of multi-word units, such as non-literal English phrasal verbs (PVs), which are particularly challenging for L2 learners to master. This eye-tracking study investigated how contextual richness influences L2 learners’ processing and acquisition of non-literal English PVs. Fifty-seven Chinese-L1 postgraduate students were randomly assigned to three groups, each reading eight low-frequency PVs in contexts varying in informativeness: more informative , less informative and uninformative. Vocabulary post-tests and delayed post-tests assessed incidental learning gains. Results indicated that more informative contexts enhanced form retention, whereas less informative contexts facilitated meaning recognition. These findings contribute to cognitive theories of word learning and offer practical insights for L2 vocabulary instruction.
papers.authors: Tianjiao Song, Barry Lee Reynolds

papers.title: The impact of early multiple language exposure on hyperactivity/inattention symptom trajectories during childhood: Results from a UK birth cohort
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Inattention and hyperactivity are common in childhood, yet their developmental trajectories vary widely. This study examines whether early multiple language exposure (MLE) is associated with hyperactivity/inattention symptoms using data from 13,175 participants in the UK Millennium Cohort Study. MLE, reported by parents at age 3, and symptoms, measured with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire at ages 5, 7 and 11, were analysed through growth mixture modelling. Four trajectory classes were identified: low-stable, high-decreasing, low-increasing, and high-stable symptoms. Children with early MLE were more likely to belong to the high-decreasing than to either the low-increasing class or the high-stable class, even after adjusting for cognitive ability and socio-demographic factors. These findings indicate an association between early MLE and trajectory membership, after adjustment for cognitive ability and socio-demographic/family factors. Given the observational design and the coarse, parent-reported assessment of MLE, interpretations about mechanisms or applied implications should remain cautious.
papers.authors: Efstathios Papachristou, Roberto Filippi, Margaret Mcavoy, Agnieszka Kałdonek-Crnjaković

papers.title: Unexpected objects increase name use: effects of implicit causality and grammatical role on L2 referential production
papers.abstract_text: Abstract L2 processing accounts differ in how predictability (i.e., the likelihood of the next mention) affects referential form choice. This study examined whether L2 learners use predictability when selecting referential forms. A story continuation experiment, manipulating grammatical role and verbs’ implicit causality (IC), tested Japanese learners of English and L1-English speakers. Learners produced fewer pronouns than L1 speakers, consistent with cross-linguistic influence from L1 Japanese. Across groups, grammatical role strongly influenced referential form choice, whereas IC-based predictability affected object references only, specifically increasing the use of names for unexpected objects. Overall, L1 and L2 speakers showed similar effects of predictability, but the effects were more limited and form-specific than grammatical role effects. Under the present task conditions, the findings are compatible with a graded, memory-interference account: Predictability is used when cues are accessible and retrieval demands are modest, yielding similar patterns in L1 and L2 referential production.
papers.authors: Masaya Hosoda

papers.title: Virtual reality (VR) for language processing and learning: Methods and approaches
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Virtual reality (VR) is a transformative technology for studying language processing and learning. It offers realistic and naturalistic environments while maintaining experimental control, supporting the exploration of social and sensorimotor cues that have often been overlooked in traditional psycholinguistic research. It can also be integrated with behavioral and neurocognitive measures to examine how learning processes influence learning outcomes. These VR characteristics have brought new opportunities and contributed to the expansion of theoretical frameworks on language processing and learning. Through reviewing recent empirical findings, we establish VR as a novel methodology for investigating how embodied and social experiences shape language processing and learning. We emphasize that realizing this potential fully requires real-time multimodal tracking of learning processes, systematic examination of individual differences and development of richer virtual environments and VR-suitable assessment tasks. This review provides methodological insights for future VR research on the neurocognitive bases of language processing and learning.
papers.authors: Zhe Gao, Shaoyun Yu, Jiayan Zhao, Shufan Yu, Suiping Wang, Ping Li

papers.title: A network analysis of the relationship between foreign language anxiety and listening fatigue in Arabic and Chinese learners of English
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Network analysis assessed the relationship between listening fatigue (Vanderbilt Listening Fatigue Scale; VFS) and foreign language learning anxiety (Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale; FLCAS). Nodes represented the questions on each scale, and edges between nodes represented the strength and direction of the correlation between those questions/nodes. A simple correlation of the sum scores revealed a negative correlation: students reporting high fatigue reported low anxiety. This result may be due to the way in which cognitive resources are allocated (i.e., “ego depletion”). Analysis of the micro- and meso-level structure of the network revealed two distinct subsets of nodes (i.e., communities), with one community containing many of the FLCAS items (and the 5 nodes highest in strength) and the other community containing the VFS items and several items from the FLCAS that assessed confidence in using L2 rather than anxiety in learning L2. Additional ways that network science can be used to increase our understanding of language learning are discussed.
papers.authors: Faisal Aljasser, Yusen Wang, Michael Vitevitch

papers.title: A quest for a unitary explanation of the object disadvantage in incremental processing: evidence from a modified maze task with Italian relative clauses
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study investigates incremental processing of subject and object relatives in Italian by comparing two experimental paradigms. Previous research has shown that object relatives are more difficult to process than subject relatives, but the source and timing of this object disadvantage remain debated. Two experiments were conducted using the same linguistic stimuli. Experiment 1 employed a novel mixed design: a lexical maze task for the relative clause combined with a self-paced reading task for the matrix clause. Experiment 2 used a self-paced reading paradigm. Results confirmed a disadvantage for object relatives across both tasks. Critically, the modified maze task revealed that this difficulty emerges immediately after the complementizer and persists in later regions, a finding that was not evident in the self-paced reading task or in previous maze task studies. This shows the greater temporal resolution of the maze paradigm for identifying the locus of syntactic difficulty in incremental processing. Although frequency-based surprisal and memory-based integration accounts explain portions of data, we consider two approaches that can offer a unified account for both early and late effects: an extension of featural relativized minimality and the cue-based retrieval account. We conclude by indicating how future research can disentangle the two accounts.
papers.authors: Mauro Viganò, Carlo Toneatto, Carlo Cecchetto

papers.title: Associations between music perception and the production of acoustic cues to lexical stress in Mandarin learners of English
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Prior work has suggested that musical abilities are associated with second language (L2) learning at both segmental and prosodic levels: For example, musicians are better at encoding lexical tone or stress in an L2 than non-musicians are. However, it remains unclear how the weighting of distinct acoustic cues when producing L2 prosody may be supported by musical abilities. Our current study investigated two different sub-domains of music perception, melody and rhythm, and their link to the accurate production of English lexical stress by native Mandarin speakers, as measured by differences from native English speakers in duration, F0, and amplitude. Melody, but not rhythm perception (and controlling for other speech perception skills, including the perception of lexical stress), significantly contributed to the production of duration and was also marginally predictive of amplitude, but not F0 production. We argue that the weak or null effects of music perception on F0 production may be due to Mandarin speakers’ F0 sensitivity from their native language, which may complicate the mapping of auditory perception onto L2 speech production skills. Results suggest complex associations between music and language in learners’ use of specific acoustic cues in their production of L2 prosody.
papers.authors: Xizi Deng, Cathy Lin, H. Henny Yeung

papers.title: Be precise if you must: Asymmetric patterns in the comprehension and production of distributivity across development
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Sentences with plural expressions can be ambiguous between a collective interpretation, where a group of agents acts together on a single object, and a distributive interpretation, where individual members act separately on different objects. Previous studies have identified developmental differences in both interpretation preferences and the use of distributive markers such as universal quantifiers: adults prefer collective interpretations, while children show no clear preference between readings; moreover, children struggle with distributive quantifiers in both comprehension and production, while adults reliably use them when needed. This study is the first to compare both comprehension preferences and production patterns across three age groups: Italian-speaking preschoolers, second graders, and adults. In a picture selection task, participants chose between collective and distributive pictures in response to unmarked, distributive, or collective sentences. In a production task, they described scenes depicting either collective or distributive actions. Results showed that all groups—including, surprisingly, preschoolers—accurately comprehended both distributive and collective markers and interpreted unmarked sentences as collective. However, in production, adults and second graders were more likely to explicitly mark distributive rather than collective interpretations, while preschoolers rarely used any disambiguating expressions. We argue that these findings reflect a developmental shift in pragmatic competence rather than in lexical knowledge, contributing new insights into the interface between semantics, pragmatics, and language development.
papers.authors: Chiara Saponaro, Desiré Carioti, Maria Teresa Guasti

papers.title: Comparing morphosyntactic and semantic-pragmatic competence in Polish-English bilinguals: Toward a Language-neutral assessment
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Evidence that certain semantic and pragmatic skills follow a similar developmental trajectory cross-linguistically suggests an important role for semantic-pragmatic tasks in the assessment of bilingual children. This study investigates whether quantifiers constitute a language-neutral linguistic category in this context. Forty-three Polish–English bilingual children aged 4–7 years completed the Quantifier Comprehension Task (QCT) and the Test for Reception of Grammar (TROG-2), a standardized morphosyntactic assessment, in both languages. The results indicated that children’s performance on QCT is strongly correlated between their two languages. This correlation was significantly stronger than that observed for the TROG-2, indicating that quantifier comprehension may be less language dependent than general grammar comprehension measures. These findings highlight the diagnostic value of semantic-pragmatic tasks, particularly quantifier interpretation, in evaluating bilingual language development. While the children in this study are all typically developing bilinguals, our goal is to explore whether quantifier comprehension tasks can support the development of language-neutral tools for assessing bilingual language skills.
papers.authors: Aneta Miękisz, Chris Cummins, Özge Öztürk, Ewa Haman, Napoleon Katsos

papers.title: Effects of stuttering and sound avoidance on reference production and memory
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Adults who stutter (AWS) frequently engage in language monitoring to anticipate and manage stuttering. This linguistic monitoring may reallocate cognitive resources, with potential consequences for language production and memory. We investigated whether AWS’ increased monitoring during production imposes dual-task costs that limit encoding benefits, or whether it enhances memory through deeper conceptual engagement. Thirty-two AWS and sixty-four adults who do not stutter (AWNS) completed a referential communication task in which they described or identified pictures with an experimenter. To simulate AWS’ linguistic monitoring, half of the AWNS performed a simultaneous sound avoidance task (AWNS-SA), prohibiting certain word-initial phonemes. After the communication task, participants completed a recognition memory test for past referents. Results showed that AWS performed more similarly to AWNS than to AWNS-SA in both language production and memory, although AWS’ memory declined on a trial-by-trial basis when stuttering occurred. These findings suggest that linguistic monitoring in AWS does not impose substantial dual-task costs overall, but that stuttering moments can transiently disrupt memory encoding. Together, these results highlight the adaptive nature of linguistic monitoring in AWS and contribute to a broader understanding of how it supports language production and memory across AWS and AWNS.
papers.authors: Si On Yoon, Morgan Schuchard, Anu Subramanian, Naomi H. Rodgers

papers.title: Features predicting item difficulty in English and Spanish elision task
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Phonological awareness (PA) is a foundational skill in early literacy acquisition across languages, including English and Spanish. While previous research has explored how factors such as word structure, phoneme characteristics, syllable stress, and syllable complexity influence PA item difficulty, the relative impact of these features—and how they may operate similarly or differently across languages—remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated the linguistic and task-format features that contribute to item difficulty in an elision task and compares these effects in English and Spanish. Using adaptive LASSO regression and dominance analysis, the study identified three significant predictors of item difficulty in English and six in Spanish. In both languages, the medial position of the deleted segment and the use of expressive response formats are the strongest predictors of increased item difficulty. In Spanish, items that produce nonwords involve longer phonological structures or require syllable deletion are associated with higher difficulty, whereas initial segment deletion tends to be easier. For English, word-level elision is associated with lower difficulty. Together, these findings highlight important considerations for designing more linguistically sensitive PA assessments in both English and Spanish.
papers.authors: Mónica Zegers, Julian M. Siebert, Lillian K. Durán, Javier Jasso, Amy S. Pratt, Jeremy Lichtmacher, Heather Murphy, Francesca Pei, Maria Luisa Gorno-Tempini

papers.title: Heritage bilingualism and language processing disparities: Spanish influence on Kaqchikel Mayan word production and sentence structures
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study examined the enduring influence of societal Spanish dominance on the indigenous Kaqchikel Mayan heritage language through three experiments with native Kaqchikel speakers. The experiments assessed word production and the processing of transitive and interrogative sentences in both Kaqchikel and Spanish. In Experiment 1, Kaqchikel speakers produced more words in Spanish than in their heritage language, indicating Spanish dominance in lexical access and suggesting a possible shift in language dominance. Given Kaqchikel’s traditional VOS (verb–object–subject) order and Spanish’s predominant SVO (subject–verb–object) order, Experiment 2a showed that in Kaqchikel, SVO sentences were processed with slightly higher accuracy than VOS sentences. In Experiment 2b for Spanish, SVO sentences were processed significantly faster than VOS sentences. Experiment 3 investigated subject (who, SquestVO) and object (whom, OquestVS) questions. In Kaqchikel (Experiment 3a), no significant differences were found in accuracy or reaction time between the two structures. In Spanish (Experiment 3b), SquestVO sentences were processed more accurately and quickly than OquestVS sentences. Overall, Kaqchikel appears to be influenced by Spanish with a general reduction in the VOS advantage and becoming more sensitive to SVO instead. These findings highlight the strong influence of Spanish on language processing among Kaqchikel speakers and reveal clear disparities between the two languages.
papers.authors: Katsuo Tamaoka, Kyoko Hayakawa, Michael P. Mansbridge, Kexin Xiong, Masatoshi Koizumi, Rinus G. Verdonschot

papers.title: How do L1 and L2 players read subtitles in video games? An exploratory eye-movement study
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Video games are prevalent and provide interactive reading platforms for learning. Despite its popularity and pedagogical potential, little is known about how players from different language backgrounds read text in video games. This exploratory study recruited 104 participants, including 56 first-language (L1) English speakers and 48 second-language (L2) English learners, who played the tutorial chapter of a commercial video game while their eye movements were recorded. The results showed that, at the subtitle level, L2 players had higher fixation counts and longer saccades than L1 players. At the word level, the word frequency effect was stronger among L2 players than L1 players in both early- and late-stage linguistic processing, as indicated by longer fixations on lower-frequency words. These eye-movement patterns suggest that L2 players adopted a more in-depth and effortful scanning strategy than L1 players when sampling textual information in gameplay. A similar lexical processing pattern was also found in an exploratory analysis of L2 players with different levels of L2 proficiency, further indicating the importance of vocabulary size for efficient lexical processing. The findings provide empirical insights into reading theories and practices related to digital reading.
papers.authors: Haiting Lan, Jan-Louis Kruger, Michael J. Richardson

papers.title: Iconicity does not always facilitate complex sentence comprehension: Behavioral and pupillometric evidence from Mandarin–English bilingual adults
papers.abstract_text: Abstract English adverbial sentences allow flexible clause ordering: main-adverbial and adverbial-main, and their comprehension by English monolingual speakers is influenced by iconicity. Iconic sentences, whose clause order reflects the chronological sequence of real-world events, are more easily comprehended (“We ate dinner before we went to see a movie”; “After we ate dinner, we went to see a movie”) than non-iconic sentences where the order of the clauses does not match the order of events in the real world (“Before we went to see a movie, we ate dinner”; “We went to see a movie after we ate dinner”). However, Mandarin speakers strongly prefer the adverbial-main order in spontaneous Mandarin speech. This paper examines whether iconicity represents a generally preferred strategy for interpreting English adverbial sentences or whether a speaker’s first language affects processing. In two studies, we tested the comprehension of English before - and after -sentences by Mandarin-English bilingual and English monolingual adults, using online pupillometry with offline accuracy in a sentence-picture matching task. We found that bilinguals, like monolinguals, comprehended after -sentences in the iconic adverbial-main order (also the preferred order in Mandarin) more accurately and with less effort than in the reverse order. However, unlike monolinguals, bilinguals did not comprehend before -sentences better in either the iconic main-adverbial order or the preferred adverbial-main order for Mandarin. Our results suggest that iconicity is not universal; instead, language-specific usage patterns, such as preferred clause order, compete with iconicity to influence processing of adverbial sentences.
papers.authors: Shijie Zhang, Alissa Ferry, Silke Brandt, Emily Warren, Anna Theakston

papers.title: Language fairness for all: Inclusive writing reduces male-default bias in adolescents across reading levels
papers.abstract_text: Abstract The current study investigates whether inclusive writing (IW), specifically full doublets (FD), that explicitly mention both masculine and feminine forms (e.g., les étudiants [masc.] et les étudiantes [fem.] | male students and female students), can reduce male-default bias in adolescents’ mental representations, and whether reading fluency or gender moderates this effect. One hundred and nine French-speaking adolescents (mean age = 12.1 years), with a broad range of reading abilities, produced lists of YouTubers and influencers under either masculine or FD instruction. Results from mixed-effects models revealed that FD significantly increased the proportion of female figures named, compared to the masculine condition, independently of reading fluency. Girls generated more female exemplars than boys, but there was no interaction with instruction type. These findings suggest that FD effectively reshape referential processing in adolescence, even for less fluent readers, by facilitating the activation of feminine exemplars in working memory and guiding referential resolution. Practically, this demonstrates that brief linguistic interventions can influence social cognition across diverse literacy profiles. Our study bridges developmental, social, and psycholinguistic perspectives, offering scalable, low-cost strategies to promote gender equity. Future work should compare FD with other inclusive formats and examine online processing costs (e.g., via eye-tracking) in educational contexts.
papers.authors: Morgane Burnel, Marjorie Guillou, Lauriane Véron-Delor

papers.title: Memory effects of implicit and explicit negation in free recall and non-verbal recognition tests
papers.abstract_text: Abstract The study investigates the memory effects of explicit and implicit negation used to inform about the absence of objects. Existing research indicates that negation can lead to incorrect recognition of negated objects as present (a negation-to-affirmation shift— NAS ). Moreover, explicit and implicit negation leads to similar memory recognition errors. The current study broadens the scope of this research by including non-verbal recognition and free recall tests. In two experiments, participants were exposed to source material containing explicit or implicit negation, and their memory was assessed using a non-verbal recognition (Experiment 1) or a free recall test (Experiment 2). In both experiments, the quality of recall was not different between explicit and implicit negation. The results are consistent with accounts of negation processing that involve simulation-based representations. In a non-verbal recognition test, the NAS effect was replicated.
papers.authors: Martyna Sekulak, Józef Maciuszek, Mateusz Polak

papers.title: Mind over print: Cognitive predictors of the ability to communicate referentially
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Communication often hinges on our ability to describe and explain things clearly so others can understand them. While this ability develops throughout childhood, little is known about how it is shaped in adulthood. This gap matters, as referential communication is central to everyday social and professional interactions. This study examines how nonverbal intelligence, formal education, literacy, and theory of mind (ToM) predict referential communication performance in adults. Forty female Spanish-speaking adults in Monterrey, Mexico—20 low-SES and 20 high-SES—completed a referential communication task along with measures of reading fluency, print exposure, nonverbal IQ, and ToM (false-belief and faux-pas tasks). Results revealed that IQ, years of education, and faux-pas comprehension significantly predicted referential communication scores. Our findings suggest that referential clarity in adult speech may rely less on reading experience and more on cognitive ability, opportunities to practice referential communication, and sensitivity to social norms and intentions. We discuss the implications of these findings.
papers.authors: Vania De la Garza, Ewa Dabrowska, Tan Arda Gedik

papers.title: Morphological processing in the parafovea during sentence reading for deaf and hearing readers
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Evidence of parafoveal preprocessing of morphology is mixed for typical hearing readers of English: they demonstrate a preview benefit from morphology for suffixed words but not for compound or prefixed words. Deaf readers may process morphological structure more efficiently in the parafovea due to their ability to attend to information further into the periphery and their particularly tight connections between orthography and semantics, which support morphological processing during initial word recognition. Morphological awareness has been shown to influence reading skill for both deaf and hearing readers, but little is known about how it affects their online processing during sentence reading. Using a gaze-contingent display change paradigm, we tested whether deaf and hearing readers with varying morphological awareness skills showed differences in parafoveal processing of morphology during sentence reading. We found that deaf readers with high morphological awareness showed a graded preview effect, with shorter gaze durations on target words (“sadness”) following a pseudomorphological preview (“sadment”) compared to a nonmorphological preview (“sadnard”). Hearing readers were unaffected by the morphological preview, regardless of skill level. These results suggest that deaf readers are attuned to morphological structure in the parafovea during sentence reading, but only if they have a higher level of morphological awareness.
papers.authors: Emily Saunders, Karen Emmorey, Elizabeth Schotter

papers.title: Older, wiser, linguistically savvy: A comparative experimental study of grammatical evidentiality across younger and older generations in Turkish and Korean Speakers
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study explores whether the ability to process grammatical evidentiality is compromised in older adults speaking Turkish and Korean, two languages that grammatically encode evidentiality. Building on previous research that suggests cognitive demands associated with language structures may reduce processing capacity in older adults, we conducted self-paced reading experiments using sentence contexts involving grammatical evidentials. We tested adult groups of young ( N = 44, ages 19–27) and older ( N = 37, ages 48–70) speakers of Korean and young ( N = 31, ages 18–31) and older ( N = 42, ages 50–85) speakers of Turkish. The results indicate that both language groups rated mismatched evidential verb forms as unacceptable, with Turkish speakers more likely to interpret mismatches as acceptable than Korean speakers. Notably, older Korean adults exhibited longer reading times (RTs) for direct evidential mismatches, while older Turkish adults showed longer RTs for indirect evidential verbs, suggesting age-related disruptions in processing. The findings only partially support the hypothesis that predicts grammatical processing differences in older compared to younger adults.
papers.authors: Seçkin Arslan, Sook Whan Cho, Miseon Lee, Semra Selvi Balo, Sun-Young Lee, Sumi Lee, Heesun Yeom, İlknur Maviş, Fanny Meunier, Say Young Kim

papers.title: On the acceptability of agreeing infinitives in Brazilian Portuguese
papers.abstract_text: Abstract We examine the acceptability of agreeing infinitivals in Brazilian Portuguese (BP) using an offline Bi-modal Acceptability Judgment Task (B-AJT) based on Modesto (2018. Complement clauses in Portuguese: Syntax and acquisition (pp. 59–129). John Benjamins.), originally designed to test the Movement Theory of Control (MTC, e.g., Hornstein 1999. Linguistic Inquiry , 30, 69–96.). Following the MTC, subject raising and subject-control sentences are analyzed uniformly within a formal syntactic paradigm (e.g., Chomsky 1995. The minimalist program . MIT Press. et sequens ). Rodrigues and Hornstein (2013. Syntax , 16(3), 292–309.) argue that intuitions on agreeing infinitives in BP in Modesto (2018. Complement clauses in Portuguese: Syntax and acquisition (pp. 59–129). John Benjamins.) are inconclusive and not worthy of serious consideration, thus neutralizing a would-be challenge to the MTC. We examine acceptability data from BP speakers ( n = 52) living in the Southeastern US, which reveal a statistically significant difference ( p < 0.029) in the acceptability of partial control (PC, m = 1.68/4) and no-control (NC) sentences ( m = 2.26/4) with agreeing infinitives. We interpret this to be indicative of robust intuitions related to sentence structures with agreeing infinitives. The validity of such intuition data lends further credence to Merchant and Gupton (2025. Journal of Linguistics , 61(2), 301–337.), which reveals significant processing differences between control and raising structures, which is unexpected under the MTC account. Linear regression results reveal a correlation between geographic region and acceptability, highlighting the importance of geographic variation, which can reveal subtle microparametric differences within languages.
papers.authors: Timothy Gupton, Doug Merchant

papers.title: Online pronoun resolution in children with developmental language disorder (DLD): A visual world eye-tracking study
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Children with Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) often experience difficulties with morphosyntax and discourse processing, which hinder their ability to establish referential coherence. While pronoun resolution has been extensively studied in typically developing (TD) children, little is known about how children with DLD process pronouns in real time, especially in Spanish—a language with rich morphology and flexible word order. This study investigated how Spanish-speaking children with DLD interpret third-person subject pronouns during sentence comprehension, examining their use of semantic and syntactic cues in reference resolution. Across three eye-tracking experiments, we tested children’s reliance on semantic gender cues in overt pronouns (Experiment 1), on syntactic cues such as grammatical role and order of mention in overt pronouns (Experiment 2), and on these same cues in null pronouns (Experiment 3). Participants were 48 Spanish–Catalan bilingual children: 16 with DLD, 16 age-matched TD peers, and 16 younger TD children matched by mean length of utterance. Eye movements during a visual world task were analyzed using growth curve and mixed-effects models. Results showed that children with DLD used semantic gender cues when available and relied on first-mentioned or subject referents when such cues were absent, suggesting compensatory use of structural heuristics in pronoun resolution.
papers.authors: Llorenç Andreu, Aurora Bel, Ernesto Guerra, Nadia Ahufinger, Monica Sanz-Torrent

papers.title: Orthographic representations in American Sign Language fingerspelling
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study examined fingerspelling accuracy and error patterns in deaf American Sign Language (ASL) signers and written spelling in hearing English speakers to investigate how orthographic representations are shaped by phonological, visual, and motor encoding strategies. Deaf participants ( n = 39) completed a fingerspelling repetition task, while hearing participants ( n = 35) completed a written dictation task using the same word and pseudoword stimuli. While overall accuracy did not differ significantly between groups, deaf participants exhibited qualitatively distinct error patterns, including higher rates of deletions and transpositions, compared to hearing participants who made more substitution errors. Deaf participants also produced more pronunciation-violating errors. Notably, they showed greater accuracy in preserving geminate (double letter) segments, highlighting enhanced sensitivity to letter identity and quantity, likely supported by the explicit visual-motor representation of geminates in fingerspelling. Additionally, deaf participants showed no difference in accuracy between real words and pseudowords, indicating that fingerspelling strategies generalized beyond stored lexical forms. We interpret these findings in light of graphemic buffer constraints, motoric fluency pressures, and the structural affordances of the fingerspelling system. Visually based encoding strategies can support robust orthographic representations for those who rely less on speech-based phonological coding.
papers.authors: Zed Sehyr, Lauren Fillet, Kiana Billot-Vasquez, Emily Saunders, Karen Emmorey

papers.title: Representation characteristics of English psych verbs in Chinese-English bilinguals: The modulating role of language proficiency
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study investigates the semantic representation of English psych verbs in Chinese-English bilinguals (CEBs) and how L2 proficiency modulates this process. A total of 180 CEBs, divided into low-, intermediate-, and high-proficiency groups, completed two masked priming experiments. Experiment 1 examined intralanguage semantic processing (synonym/antonym associations, word frequency effects) and found that high-proficiency learners showed a significant processing facilitation for high-frequency synonyms over antonyms, reflecting robust facilitation of high-frequency synonym priming. Experiment 2 explored interlanguage processing via Chinese-English (C-E)/English-Chinese (E-C) translation equivalents and word frequency, showing that low-proficiency participants exhibited the largest translation priming effects, particularly for high-frequency words in the C-E direction. Across all proficiency levels, intralanguage processing was generally faster than interlanguage processing, whereas interlanguage priming effects tended to be more pronounced overall. These findings reveal proficiency-dependent shifts in the interaction between semantic and frequency information, highlight translation equivalence as a core mechanism in bilingual semantic organization, and refine the distributed feature model and the shared asymmetric model by demonstrating their applicability to abstract verb categories beyond the concrete nouns on which they were originally developed.
papers.authors: Yun Wang, Xinfang Liu

papers.title: Sprouts of literacy: The longitudinal prediction of early morphological awareness skills in French
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Morphological awareness, i.e., the ability to consciously manipulate roots (e.g., HEALTH ) and affixes (e.g., -Y as in HEALTHY ), is a key skill for literacy development. While its role is well documented from Grade 3 onward, its early contribution to reading and spelling acquisition remains unclear, especially in French. This study investigates whether morphological awareness predicts early reading and spelling, particularly for derived and inconsistent words, from Grade 1. We used an accelerated longitudinal design with two cohorts of French-speaking children ( N = 291): one from Grade 1 to 2 and the other from Grade 2 to 3. An autoregressive structural equation model (SEM) was used to examine the predictive role of morphological awareness on later literacy outcomes, controlling for phonological skills, vocabulary, and non-verbal reasoning. Morphological awareness significantly predicted general reading and spelling abilities, and specifically the spelling of derived words, but not their reading. These effects were stronger in the younger cohort (Grade 1 to 2) due to the lesser effect of the autoregressive path. Morphological awareness plays a unique role in early literacy, particularly in spelling morphologically complex words. Findings are discussed in light of French orthographic consistency and current models of literacy acquisition.
papers.authors: Estelle Ardanouy, Pascal Zesiger, Hélène Delage, Elise Lefèvre

papers.title: The impact of task demand on subtitle reading in video games: an eye-tracking study
papers.abstract_text: Abstract While prior research has established how people read in non-interactive media, little is known about the reading process in interactive multimedia such as video games. In this exploratory eye-tracking study, two levels of reading demand (high vs. low) were created during gameplay. Ninety-eight participants were randomly assigned to play a video game with either an English (L1; low reading demand) or an unintelligible foreign-language (FL; high reading demand) soundtrack. At the subtitle level, the FL group (vs. the L1 group) had higher dwell time percentages, more fixations, higher regression rates, and longer mean fixation durations. No group differences were found in saccade lengths. At the word level, the FL group skipped fewer words. An interaction was found between reading demand and word frequency, where the magnitude of skipping lower-frequency words (vs. higher-frequency words) was smaller in the FL group. Gaze duration showed a significant word frequency effect only. The FL group had longer total fixation time on words, and no interaction was found. These results showed that the FL group (vs. the L1 group) experienced greater processing efforts, as reflected in increased fixation-based measures and regressions. The current study provided empirical insights into task-driven reading in interactive multimedia.
papers.authors: Haiting Lan, Jan-Louis Kruger, Michael Richardson

papers.title: The processing advantage of emotion words in L1 speakers and L2 speakers: A meta-analysis
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This meta-analysis synthesized 88 studies to investigate the processing advantages of emotion words over neutral words. Additionally, we explored the moderating effects of emotional properties (valence, arousal, emotion word type), linguistic factors (concreteness, frequency, length, neighborhood size), and task type in L1, advanced L2, and intermediate L2 speakers. We found a significant valence effect, with positive words showing a greater processing advantage than negative words only in L1 speakers. For arousal, the interaction analysis revealed that high arousal reduced the processing advantage of emotion words to a greater extent in intermediate L2 speakers than in L1 speakers. Furthermore, only advanced L2 speakers showed a significant processing advantage for emotion-label words compared to emotion-laden words. Regarding linguistic factors, longer word length was associated with greater processing advantages compared to shorter word length, but only in advanced L2 speakers. The greater processing advantage for concrete over abstract emotion words was observed only in intermediate L2 speakers, indicating that this group was the most sensitive to concreteness among all language speaker groups. Finally, task type significantly influenced emotion word processing in interaction with language proficiency. Overall, our findings support theoretical frameworks in both L1 and L2 processing and cognition.
papers.authors: Yanlu Zhong, Lu Liu, Laurel Brehm

papers.title: The role of perceptual salience in L2 morphology acquisition: Attention, awareness, and intake
papers.abstract_text: Abstract Acquiring morphology poses a considerable challenge in second language acquisition (SLA), highlighting the need to explore methods that facilitate this task for L2 learners. One potential facilitator is salience, which is theorized to aid language acquisition by directing learners’ attention to certain linguistic elements. To empirically investigate the impact of one type of salience, perceptual salience, a text-based eye-tracking experiment was conducted with 68 L1 Dutch speakers who read 240 sentences in Englishti , an English-based semi-artificial language featuring perceptually high-salient ( -ulp ) and low-salient ( -o ) morphemes according to length. Learning context was manipulated with participants being either assigned to an intentional or an incidental paradigm. The task consisted of two phases: a learning phase involving input flooding of the target morphemes followed by content-related questions, and a testing phase where participants completed a grammaticality judgment task on Englishti sentences, half of which were familiar from the learning phase and half of which were new. The results revealed a significant influence of salience, mediated by learning context and English proficiency, on fixation durations, thus empirically confirming the effect of perceptual salience on attention allocation in L2 morphology acquisition.

papers.title: The role of pitch statistical learning in second language morphosyntactic acquisition
papers.abstract_text: Abstract To contribute to the ongoing discussion on the role of pitch processing in grammar learning, this study examines the extent to which pitch statistical learning (pitch statistical learning (SL); the ability to detect and internalize pitch patterns in auditory input) affects second language (L2) morphosyntax learning outcomes. In the context of 93 Japanese learners of English, piece-wise regression analyses were conducted to compare the roles of their pitch SL abilities and pitch acuity in L2 morphosyntactic knowledge. The results revealed a weak but significant positive correlation between pitch SL and morphosyntactic knowledge, whereas pitch acuity showed no significant association. Further analysis identified a threshold effect: pitch SL has a strong association with morphosyntactic knowledge for learners with lower pitch SL abilities, but not for those with higher pitch SL abilities. These findings suggest that the lack of pitch SL ability could substantially slow down L2 morphosyntactic learning.

papers.title: Variable bilingual experiences and their influence on a contextualized acceptability judgment task
papers.abstract_text: Abstract This study examines the relationship between code-switching (CS) experience, as measured by the Bilingual Code-Switching Profile (BCSP), and ratings from an acceptability judgment task (AJT). Although the BCSP offers a structured way to quantify bilinguals’ CS behavior, its application in grammaticality studies and its ability to reflect bilingual heterogeneity have been underexamined. We address this by asking: (1) How do BCSP scores predict acceptability ratings of Spanish–English CS sentences? and (2) How do BCSP scores reflect the social heterogeneity of US bilingual populations, focusing on age, gender, region, place of birth, and national origin? A total of 137 Latinx bilinguals across the USA completed an online survey including the BCSP and 40 reggaetón-inspired CS sentences, balanced for grammaticality and experimental label (i.e., Source: Reggaetón lyrics). Results from multilevel and linear regression models indicate that higher BCSP scores are associated with higher AJT ratings, particularly among participants who report frequent CS use, greater proficiency, and positive attitudes. Social variables had limited impact, although age and place of birth emerged as modest predictors. These findings highlight the BCSP’s value in capturing CS experience and stress the need to account for bilingual variability in studies of acceptability judgments.

papers.title: A Communicative–Linguistic Analysis of Typically Developing Children Aged 12- to 37-Month-Old Using the Dynamic Communication Evaluation Coding Scheme: Data Presentation and Comparison Across Age Groups
papers.abstract_text: This study collected cross-sectional data on the social, communicative, pragmatic, and linguistic abilities of typically developing 12- to 37-month-old children. A preliminary literature review indicated that no observational tool with robust psychometric properties is currently available to assess communication and language in this age range. To address this gap, a coding scheme was employed on data from 91 typically developing Italian children (all with expressive vocabulary above the 10th percentile), who were divided into 3 groups (G1:12–17 months; G2:18–23 months; G3:24–37 months). Videotaped parent–child play interactions were analyzed to assess communicative frequency, gaze-related communicative prerequisites, communicative roles, communicative functions, and language complexity. Significant group differences and correlations with age and vocabulary were identified, including a reduction in assertiveness and requesting functions and an increase in responsiveness and declarative functions. The developmental progression of linguistic complexity is consistent with the previous literature, supporting the validity of the study and offering implications for both clinical practice and research.

papers.title: Advanced Theory of Mind in Syrian Arabic–Turkish Sequential Bilinguals and Turkish Monolinguals: Assessment Language, School-Language Attainment, and the Ecology of Bilingualism
papers.abstract_text: Claims about bilingual advantages in children’s social cognition remain unsettled, particularly when language proficiency and context are taken seriously. This study examined advanced theory of mind in Syrian Arabic–Turkish sequential bilinguals in Türkiye. One hundred bilingual children (11–12 years) and 50 Turkish monolingual peers completed the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test–Child (RMET) and the Faux Pas Recognition Test–Child; bilinguals were randomly assigned to Arabic or Turkish assessment. Monolinguals outperformed bilinguals on RMET, Faux Pas, control, and total Faux Pas scores. Within the bilingual sample, Turkish assessment improved RMET performance but not Faux Pas performance. These patterns remained after adjustment for age, nonverbal reasoning, Turkish attainment, preschool duration, and household size. The findings suggest that advanced social-cognitive performance in immigrant bilinguals is shaped less by language status alone than by school-language experience and the broader ecology in which bilingualism is lived.

papers.title: Application of Recurrent Activation Models to Mechanistic Explanations of DLD: A Commentary on Riches (2026)
papers.abstract_text: We respond to Riches’ article in which he puts forth the idea that exemplar-based learning is the underlying deficit in children with Developmental Language Disorder, grounded in Dell and Chang’s P-Chain model. We affirm the potential contributions of exemplar-based learning and explore other potential possibilities for mechanistic explanations of learning differences grounded in this model, including inhibitory control, working memory, extant knowledge, prediction error and feedback. We propose ways that these explanations might guide clinical practice.

papers.title: Applying the LUNA Framework and Global TALES Protocol for Analyzing Personal Narratives in a Cross-Linguistic Study of Predominantly English and French-Speaking 9-10-Year-Olds from Canada
papers.abstract_text: Personal narratives, stories about past personal experiences, are closely associated with social, academic, and mental health outcomes. Despite their importance, few validated assessment tools are available for Speech-Language Pathologists (SLPs) to assess personal narrative abilities. To address this gap, the Global Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories (TALES) Network developed a standardized protocol designed to support cross-cultural and cross-linguistic comparisons. This study examines the feasibility of the Global TALES protocol for eliciting personal narratives from Canadian predominantly English- and French-speaking children and compares their narrative performance across four components of discourse processing derived from the Linguistic Underpinnings of Narrative in Aphasia (LUNA) framework: linguistic, propositional, macrostructure planning, and pragmatic. Using the French or English version of the Global TALES protocol, personal narratives from 40 typically developing children aged 9 to 10 years were collected: 20 English speaking and 20 French speaking. Narrative measures included verbal productivity, lexical diversity, and syntactic complexity at the linguistic level; local coherence at the propositional level; context and chronology at the macrostructure planning level; and narrative topics and theme at the pragmatic level. The Global TALES protocol successfully elicited personal narratives across both language groups (70%–100% across the 6 prompts), and no significant differences were found between groups across all 4 discourse components of the LUNA framework, with inter-rater reliability ranging from 72.5% to 94.3%. These findings support the promise of the Global TALES protocol as a clinically relevant tool for SLPs wanting to assess personal narrative skills, alongside a comprehensive framework, while allowing for cross-linguistic and cross-cultural comparisons.
